articles.title: Trump says Putin-Zelensky meeting to be set up 'very soon'
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: "There'll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made," Mr. Trump told reporters
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) that a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky would be set up "very soon."
The announcement came as Trump's administration ramps up diplomatic efforts aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, now in its fifth year.
"There'll be a meeting set up very soon and I think a lot of progress could be made," Mr. Trump told reporters.
Mr. Zelensky said on Sunday that a trilateral meeting between Kyiv, Washington and Moscow would take place in November, aiming to restart stalled peace talks.
The Kremlin had previously said that a meeting between the three countries was planned to take place in the United Arab Emirates in November.
Mr. Putin, who ordered the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, has consistently rejected face-to-face talks with Mr. Zelensky and insisted Moscow intends to seize the rest of eastern Ukraine.
Mr. Trump came to power in January 2025 promising to end the war in 24 hours — but over a year of U.S.-led talks have failed to produce a breakthrough, with tens of thousands killed.
In recent days, Mr. Trump has once again pivoted away from Ukraine and back to Mr. Putin, trumpeting what he said was a deal for Russia to sell diesel and reduce prices sent soaring by his Iran war.

articles.title: At least 68 dead after two trains collide in Spain’s Toledo Province
articles.examRelevance: Current Affairs & GS-II: Bilateral Treaties, Global Summits (UN/G20/BRICS/Quad) & Strategic Diplomacy
fullParagraphs: The second such accident to strike Spain this year will raise fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, with the Transport Minister speaking of an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the collision.

A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed at least 68 people and injured scores more on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), with the toll likely to rise, authorities said, in one of Europe’s deadliest such disasters this century.

The second such accident to strike Spain in 2026 will raise fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, with the Transport Minister speaking of an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the collision.

AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.
Dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.
Castilla-La Mancha’s leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene that 68 people had died, raising an earlier toll of 64 and having already warned of more victims being found.
A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.

People check an information screen displaying a message that the high-speed train line between Madrid and Andalucia has been interrupted following the collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz at Atocha train station in Madrid, Spain, on October 28, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters
Pablo Mejia, 42, with blood staining his grey jumper, told AFP that he had miraculously survived after changing his seat, as he awaited a transfer to the southern city of Seville.
He recounted “a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos”.

The second such accident to strike Spain this year will raise fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, with the Transport Minister speaking of an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the collision.

A high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed at least 68 people and injured scores more on Wednesday (October 28, 2026), with the toll likely to rise, authorities said, in one of Europe’s deadliest such disasters this century.

The second such accident to strike Spain in 2026 will raise fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, with the Transport Minister speaking of an “error” and “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the collision.

AFP reporters on the scene in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha saw one train embedded into another and some carriages lying on their side in tangles of metal debris at the bottom of an embankment.

Dozens of emergency services vehicles were racing to and from the site during a frantic search for survivors, while several black vans arrived from a funeral parlour.

Castilla-La Mancha’s leader Emiliano Garcia-Page told reporters at the scene that 68 people had died, raising an earlier toll of 64 and having already warned of more victims being found.

A spokeswoman from the Castilla-La Mancha regional government told AFP that more than 100 people had been injured. Of them, 58 had been taken to hospital, with 15 in a critical condition.

State railway operator Renfe confirmed in a statement that the main high-speed line from Madrid to southern Spain had been suspended after one of its services suffered an accident with a train from private Spanish company Iryo.

People check an information screen displaying a message that the high-speed train line between Madrid and Andalucia has been interrupted following the collision of two high-speed trains between the towns of Mora and Orgaz at Atocha train station in Madrid, Spain, on October 28, 2026. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Pablo Mejia, 42, with blood staining his grey jumper, told AFP that he had miraculously survived after changing his seat, as he awaited a transfer to the southern city of Seville.

He recounted “a very strong hit. It lasted a long time until it stopped, lots of people on the floor, on top of each other, seats ripped out, suitcases, a lot of chaos”.

articles.title: Bengaluru-based Nature Classrooms releases new butterfly migration game
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Aswathi Asokan, who has conceptualised this new game, talks about its genesis, how it is played and how gamification can help drive conservation

Aswathi Asokan’s journey into the fascinating world of butterflies began in 2019, as a first-year Zoology student at Chennai’s Stella Maris College. “There were a couple of professors in the Zoology Department who were interested in the natural world,” she says, recalling how one of them, Kalpana Jayaraman, was conducting butterfly walks on campus.
“So I began joining those,” says the Bengaluru-based nature educator, researcher, and conservationist who has conceptualised Monsoon Wings, a new butterfly migration and life-cycle game.

As someone who grew up on the verdant IIT Madras campus, she always loved nature, but “it had never got to the point where I was actively identifying species,” she says. Then, on that first campus walk, the professor gave participants a simple printout of the names and pictures of eight or nine common butterflies.

“That made all the difference. Every time I saw a butterfly, I would go back to the printout and try to identify it,” says Aswathi, who developed Monsoon Wings as part of her role as the manager of curriculum development, resources & training at Nature Classrooms, a Bengaluru-based organisation that works with schools and educators to connect learning and the natural world. “I like to think that this was the start of me understanding the power of a tool like that.”

She began noticing butterflies a lot more after that, closely observing their life cycles in the plants around her. At around the same time, she became part of the Chennai Young Naturalists’ Network, a group of young naturalists in Chennai.

Through this group, she met like-minded people, with whom she would go on to co-author a bilingual field guide, Butterflies of Chennai , in 2023. ”The data used to create the guide came from my friend Vikas Madhav, an experienced young naturalist who did nearly 10 years of butterfly documentation work in Chennai before moving to the US,” says Aswathi, who ended up doing a lot of nature education work in Chennai before going on to pursue a master’s in wildlife conservation action from the Bharati Vidyapeeth Institute of Environment Education and Research, Pune.
Blue Tiger butterflies are known for their seasonal migrations, linked to monsoon cycles | Photo Credit: MURALI KUMAR K

All the time spent dabbling in resource creation, including field guides, bingos and posters, has played a tremendous role in shaping this new butterfly game, which has been inspired by the ‘Bird Survivor’ game by Early Bird, an initiative by the Education and Public Engagement Programme of the Nature Conservation Foundation. “We were using this game extensively in our Nature Classrooms workshops, and I got familiar with it,” Aswathi says, explaining that this game, in turn, took inspiration from one developed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

While working with Nature Classrooms, Aswathi was also actively working with Sunnyside Learning School in Chennai, running biodiversity exploration programmes for its students. “I was trying to plan a session around butterflies for the Sunnyside kids, and since the mechanics are quite similar, I thought I could adapt the bird migration game to a butterfly context and see if it works.”

While bird and monarch butterfly migration are well known and widely discussed, butterfly migration in India is so common right around us, yet few people know about it, Aswathi says. “That’s why I wanted to create a resource and incorporate that into the kids’ session.”

articles.title: India must build a holistic care system
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework

India’s development story over the past decade has been one of infrastructure: highways, metro lines, electrification and digital public platforms, each treated as a foundation for growth that requires public investment and planning. One foundation on which every household and economy depends has not received the same attention: care.

Everyone needs care at some point in life. How care is organised shapes people’s opportunities, well-being and participation in society and the economy. When services are absent, families, and women most of all, bear the cost in unpaid work, lost earnings, and narrower opportunities.

In the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as the main reason for staying out of the labour force. India’s Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, spending an average of 140 minutes a day on it. Expanding access to affordable, quality care services can give women greater freedom to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life. With an ageing population, the need for accessible care services will only grow.

Yet care rarely features in India’s growth strategy. For a Viksit Bharat 2047, the question is not only how to expand women’s economic participation, but how to build the care system that makes such participation possible. The Anganwadi network, strengthened through Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, anchors early childhood care and nutrition. Palna, under Mission Shakti, supports crèches, while Mission Vatsalya, social security and provisions for persons with disabilities and senior citizens address other needs. The challenge is architecture, not ambition. Four gaps stand out.

First, fragmentation. Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework. This can leave gaps such as crèches that close before factory shifts end or eldercare needs that fall outside of existing schemes.

Second, coverage. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimates that 9–10 million women in low-income urban households need childcare. Similarly for eldercare, 24% of older persons face limitations in daily activities, while national data on service availability and coverage remain limited.

Third, the workforce. Care depends on frontline workers; from Anganwadi workers to home-based caregivers and domestic workers — many of whom remain inadequately remunerated or engaged on an honorary basis. Building on NITI Aayog’s proposals, clear standards, certification, decent working conditions, social protection and career pathways would recognise care as skilled and paid work.

Finally, financing and norms. Care is still budgeted as welfare rather than investment, and workplace policies assume that caregiving is women’s work. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) recommends statutory paid paternity leave in the private sector.

Comparable economies are building their own care ecosystems. Colombia’s 2025 National Care Policy brings 34 government entities under one framework. Brazil’s 2024 National Care Policy and 2025 National Care Plan set up inter-Ministerial committees to steer implementation. In Nepal, care mapping was used to fund care pilots.

In India, NITI Aayog’s Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047 report proposes a National Caregiving Council to strengthen coordination. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. State-level care roadmaps can make this practical. States can map needs, services and demographic trends, identify gaps in childcare, eldercare and disability support, and prepare costed plans with clear responsibilities.

🚀 Science, Tech & Environment 📅 29 Oct 2026 ⏱️ 5 Min Read

📰 India must build a holistic care system

🎯 Exam Relevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
🔮 Futuristic Word Radar: Paragraph ke kisi bhi English word par Double-Click karein — turant uska Hinglish Meaning + Picture screen par dekhein!

Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework

India’s development story over the past decade has been one of infrastructure: highways, metro lines, electrification and digital public platforms, each treated as a foundation for growth that requires public investment and planning. One foundation on which every household and economy depends has not received the same attention: care.

Everyone needs care at some point in life. How care is organised shapes people’s opportunities, well-being and participation in society and the economy. When services are absent, families, and women most of all, bear the cost in unpaid work, lost earnings, and narrower opportunities.

In the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as the main reason for staying out of the labour force. India’s Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, spending an average of 140 minutes a day on it. Expanding access to affordable, quality care services can give women greater freedom to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life. With an ageing population, the need for accessible care services will only grow.

Yet care rarely features in India’s growth strategy. For a Viksit Bharat 2047, the question is not only how to expand women’s economic participation, but how to build the care system that makes such participation possible. The Anganwadi network, strengthened through Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, anchors early childhood care and nutrition. Palna, under Mission Shakti, supports crèches, while Mission Vatsalya, social security and provisions for persons with disabilities and senior citizens address other needs. The challenge is architecture, not ambition. Four gaps stand out.

First, fragmentation. Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework. This can leave gaps such as crèches that close before factory shifts end or eldercare needs that fall outside of existing schemes.

Second, coverage. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimates that 9–10 million women in low-income urban households need childcare. Similarly for eldercare, 24% of older persons face limitations in daily activities, while national data on service availability and coverage remain limited.

Third, the workforce. Care depends on frontline workers; from Anganwadi workers to home-based caregivers and domestic workers — many of whom remain inadequately remunerated or engaged on an honorary basis. Building on NITI Aayog’s proposals, clear standards, certification, decent working conditions, social protection and career pathways would recognise care as skilled and paid work.

Finally, financing and norms. Care is still budgeted as welfare rather than investment, and workplace policies assume that caregiving is women’s work. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) recommends statutory paid paternity leave in the private sector.

Comparable economies are building their own care ecosystems. Colombia’s 2025 National Care Policy brings 34 government entities under one framework. Brazil’s 2024 National Care Policy and 2025 National Care Plan set up inter-Ministerial committees to steer implementation. In Nepal, care mapping was used to fund care pilots.

In India, NITI Aayog’s Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047 report proposes a National Caregiving Council to strengthen coordination. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. State-level care roadmaps can make this practical. States can map needs, services and demographic trends, identify gaps in childcare, eldercare and disability support, and prepare costed plans with clear responsibilities.

The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. articles.title: India rejects patent bid for treatment of drug-resistant TB
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Civil society groups urge U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development to withdraw related patent claims in other countries

The Indian Patent Office has rejected a patent application filed by the U.S.-based Global Alliance for TB Drug Development (TB Alliance) for the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid (BPaL), a six-month, all-oral treatment regimen for drug-resistant tuberculosis.
The Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust and Third World Network (TWN) welcomed the development.
Recommended by the WHO for eligible people, BPaL offers a shorter course of treatment than older, longer regimens, reducing the burden of treatment on patients and their families.

“Only those who have been treated for TB know what it feels like to go through more than a year of antibiotics with painful injections. Access to a shorter, oral and effective treatment can mean returning to work, caring for their families and rebuilding their lives”, explained Loon Gangte of DNP+.

The decision follows two pre-grant oppositions filed in 2020—one by Eldred Tellis (Sankalp Rehabilitation Trust) and Ganesh Acharya, with support from the Lawyers’ Collective and Médécins Sans Frontières Access Campaign, and the other by the Delhi Network of Positive People (DNP+), with support from TWN.

The opponents challenged the patent application on the grounds that the combination of bedaquiline, pretomanid and linezolid, as well as its use in a shorter treatment regimen, had already been disclosed in scientific research and clinical trials dating back to 2015. They argued that combining these known medicines did not constitute an inventive step warranting a new patent monopoly.

The Opposition invoked key safeguards under India’s Patents Act, including Section 3(d), which restricts patents on new uses of known substances, Section 3(e), which excludes mere admixtures, and Section 3(i), which excludes methods of medical treatment. The opponents further argued that the application failed to sufficiently disclose the claimed invention. All four grounds were upheld by the Indian Patent Office.

India has the world’s largest tuberculosis burden. According to WHO estimates, approximately 2.71 million people developed TB in the country in 2024, accounting for a quarter of global cases, with an incidence rate of 187 per 1,00,000 people. Civil society groups are also demanding that the TB Alliance stop the pursuit of proprietary rights over BPaL in other countries.

“Having received public and philanthropic support to develop pretomanid, one of BPaL’s components, they should not be applying for a patent, let alone over frivolous secondary patents on its combination with the other two known medicines,” said Mr. Tellis.

In light of the weak claims by the TB Alliance, Prathibha Sivasubramanian, senior researcher at TWN, endorsed the call for the waiving of patents. “The Indian Patent Office’s decision should serve as a clear signal to the TB Alliance to voluntarily surrender granted patents and to withdraw all corresponding pending applications in other jurisdictions. TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.

TB Alliance should also publish its pretomanid licence agreements,” she said.

articles.title: Sharp cuts in price of cancer drugs expose excessive pricing, say health experts
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: NPPA releases revised MRPs for 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with the new prices effective from November 9; Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India) says controlling trade margins alone is insufficient as life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay

The revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP) list of anti-cancer medicines published by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) raises serious concerns about excessive pricing and the exploitation of patients, noted medical health activists on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
Editorial | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing

The NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has released a list of 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with their revised MRP that will be effective from November 9.

“The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to October 27, 2026, and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs,” said a release issued by the Union government on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).

On October 17, the NPPA had announced Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in public interest to address excessive trade margins, make cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines. Manufacturers were instructed to submit their revised list to NPPA.

The 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs include immunotherapy medicines used in the treatment of over 20 types of cancer, Denosumab used by breast and prostate cancer patients, Pegfilgrastim used to prevent neutropenia in cancer patients, and Bevacizumab, which is approved for the treatment of colon, ovarian and cervical cancers.

Stating that cost-based price control can further reduce medicine prices and curb excessive profiteering, Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India), an organisation working for accessibility of medicines, said that controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.

In their statement, the group explained: “For example, the reported MRP of one brand of palbociclib fell from approximately ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 per pack, while thiotepa fell from approximately ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 per vial. Such drastic reductions raise serious questions about the pricing practices of pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian manufacturers of generic cancer medicines that have reportedly offered substantial trade margins while patients continued to face unaffordable prices.’’

It added that, several patented cancer medicines remain exorbitantly priced. The Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) policy has failed to ensure affordability, while excluding medicines supplied free under Patient Assistance Programmes from its calculations has further limited its potential impact on patients, said the group.

“The policy’s formula is also deeply flawed. Allowing a 42.8% markup over the Price to Stockist [PTS] legitimises excessive margins, particularly in a supply chain often involving only one or two intermediaries or direct sales to hospitals. A substantially lower markup, comparable to the 16% margin applicable to scheduled formulations under the DPCO framework, could have delivered greater benefits to patients. A one-time MRP reduction is not enough. Without permanent, enforceable margin caps, regular monitoring and verification by NPPA, excessive pricing can persist or re-emerge,” JSA stated in the release.

NPPA releases revised MRPs for 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with the new prices effective from November 9; Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India) says controlling trade margins alone is insufficient as life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay

The revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP) list of anti-cancer medicines published by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) raises serious concerns about excessive pricing and the exploitation of patients, noted medical health activists on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).

Editorial | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing

The NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has released a list of 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with their revised MRP that will be effective from November 9.

“The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to October 27, 2026, and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs,” said a release issued by the Union government on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).

On October 17, the NPPA had announced Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in public interest to address excessive trade margins, make cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines. Manufacturers were instructed to submit their revised list to NPPA.

The 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs include immunotherapy medicines used in the treatment of over 20 types of cancer, Denosumab used by breast and prostate cancer patients, Pegfilgrastim used to prevent neutropenia in cancer patients, and Bevacizumab, which is approved for the treatment of colon, ovarian and cervical cancers.

Stating that cost-based price control can further reduce medicine prices and curb excessive profiteering, Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India), an organisation working for accessibility of medicines, said that controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.

In their statement, the group explained: “For example, the reported MRP of one brand of palbociclib fell from approximately ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 per pack, while thiotepa fell from approximately ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 per vial. Such drastic reductions raise serious questions about the pricing practices of pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian manufacturers of generic cancer medicines that have reportedly offered substantial trade margins while patients continued to face unaffordable prices.’’

It added that, several patented cancer medicines remain exorbitantly priced. The Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) policy has failed to ensure affordability, while excluding medicines supplied free under Patient Assistance Programmes from its calculations has further limited its potential impact on patients, said the group.

“The policy’s formula is also deeply flawed. Allowing a 42.8% markup over the Price to Stockist [PTS] legitimises excessive margins, particularly in a supply chain often involving only one or two intermediaries or direct sales to hospitals. A substantially lower markup, comparable to the 16% margin applicable to scheduled formulations under the DPCO framework, could have delivered greater benefits to patients. A one-time MRP reduction is not enough. Without permanent, enforceable margin caps, regular monitoring and verification by NPPA, excessive pricing can persist or re-emerge,” JSA stated in the release.

fullParagraphs: Clarification comes after Road Ministry sought audit of users accessing the Centre’s logistics portal following complaints that multiple apps and websites are selling vehicle information

After the Road Ministry sought an audit of users accessing the Centre’s logistics portal following complaints that multiple apps and websites were selling vehicle information, the Unified Logistics Interface Platform (ULIP) rejected the allegations of its misuse. It said all data were masked and called for broader scrutiny of the platforms involved.

“ULIP relays information in the format received from the source API. For example, vehicle owner names, chassis and engine numbers retain their masking, and the mobile number field remains null in both the source response and the response provided to users. ULIP does not independently generate, unmask or enrich the underlying data,” ULIP wrote in response to a story in The Hindu .

The Road Ministry sought an audit after finding that some entities were extracting data in large volumes from ULIP with some as many pulling out as many as 50 lakh records a month. The Road Ministry shares vehicle information with multiple government agencies and private firms from its portals such as VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals.

ULIP says it uses sufficient safeguards that include screening of entities that have access to its portal, their proposed use cases, binding terms and conditions, IP whitelisting, phased onboarding and continuous monitoring of API usage. This framework complies with the Road Ministry’s Policy for Data Sharing from the National Transport Repository, which prescribes authentication, secret keys, masking of personally identifiable information (PII) and defined approval mechanisms, ULIP added.

Referring to multiple apps selling vehicle information data in unmasked form, ULIP said there needed to be a “scrutiny of wider ecosystem of platforms and channels through which such information is being made available”.

The Road Ministry has written to the government’s nodal agency for investigating cybersecurity incidents, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), seeking a forensic audit of VAHAN, SARATHI, e-Challan and PUCC portals, which hold a range of vehicle-owner information.

It has also sought the intervention of the Ministry of Electronics and Information and Technology (MEITY) for a review of its data sharing policy and suggest ways to strengthen it. The Road Ministry also plans to audit various enforcement agencies that access its portals for data.

The Ministry’s action follows reports that apps and websites were selling vehicle-linked personal data for as little as ₹5. A Cyderes investigation found that a Telegram-based broker could retrieve an owner’s name, contact details, addresses and other records from a vehicle registration number, along with driving licence, challan, FASTag and registration certificate information. The Ministry has asked major app-store operators, including Google, to remove such apps.

articles.title: How imaging offers a window to treat wake-up strokes
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: One in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body

Time is brain, when it comes to the treatment of strokes. But a stroke occurring during sleep may go unnoticed until a person wakes up with symptoms, leaving doctors without a clear timeline of its onset. This is where brain imaging helps doctors identify patients with wake-up strokes and assess the extent of injury to pave the way for prompt treatment. Neurologists underscore the need to seek medical care immediately to ensure timely treatment.

M. Radha, head of department and professor of neurology, Government Kilpauk Medical College (KMC) Hospital, Chennai, said that the prevalence of wake-up strokes is 20% - one in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body,” she said.

If a patient arrives at a hospital within 4.5 hours of stroke symptoms, then thrombolysis can be done, she said, adding: “However, in wake-up stroke, we cannot calculate the time of the onset of symptoms. We do not know the window. So, acting fast is important. In case of any symptoms, patients should reach the hospital on time.”

In wake-up strokes, imaging helps give a clear picture for the doctors. “An MRI brain scan should be taken immediately. If it is not available, a CT angiogram should be taken. The scans help us assess the extent of brain injury and blood flow to different parts of the brain. They can determine whether there is diffusion-perfusion mismatch. The difference may represent brain tissue that is still salvageable and can be potentially saved. Like in regular strokes, ‘time is brain’ in wake-up strokes too, making prompt diagnosis and treatment crucial,” she explained.

Shubha Subramanian, senior consultant - neurology, Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai, said that in ischemic strokes, thrombolysis is used to dissolve the blood clot if a patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. “In cases involving a large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is performed within 24 hours of symptom onset, depending on the patient’s eligibility. In wake-up strokes, we do not know when the stroke started; it could be at night or early in the morning. What we do next is crucial. This is why we rely on imaging techniques,” she added.

“MRI has a lot of sequences. If you compare the diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) imaging, a mismatch in that shows that the brain tissue is still salvageable. So even if we do not know the time of onset of stroke, we can still go ahead and thrombolyse the patient. In the same way, MRI perfusion or CT perfusion studies will also give us a clue regarding salvageable brain tissue. This will help us in taking crucial decisions regarding thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or whether to go for conservative management,” she elaborated.

Under the Tamil Nadu Accident and Emergency Care Initiative and Stroke Care and Rapid Intervention with Plasminogen activator and Thrombectomy (SCRIPT) programme implemented by the Tamil Nadu government and with facilities available at the new JICA building at KMC, patients with with wake-up strokes are regularly treated, Dr. Radha noted.

“There is effective coordination between the administration, the emergency department, radiology and neurology departments. We have a green channel in place. As a result, once the patients with symptoms of stroke enter the Emergency Department, the neurologist is intimated. Our doctor goes to the radiology department which has significantly reduced the door to needle time,” she said.

BE FAST is the acronym to spot the warning signs of stroke, denoting Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech and Time. “We do see that the awareness of stroke symptoms is increasing and the referral system has also improved,” Dr. Radha said.

Dr. Shubha Subramanian said that in wake-up strokes, the person may not realise that he/she has symptoms of stroke when they wake up from sleep. “They may face difficulty in getting up and may also fall as a result. It is important for family members to identify the symptoms and rush for medical help,” she added.

This is where brain imaging helps doctors identify patients with wake-up strokes and assess the extent of injury to pave the way for prompt treatment. Neurologists underscore the need to seek medical care immediately to ensure timely treatment.

M. Radha, head of department and professor of neurology, Government Kilpauk Medical College (KMC) Hospital, Chennai, said that the prevalence of wake-up strokes is 20% - one in five ischaemic strokes is a wake-up stroke. “This means a person wakes up from his/her sleep with symptoms of stroke. The symptoms include facial drooping, difficulty speaking, sudden vision problems and weakness on one side of the body,” she said.

If a patient arrives at a hospital within 4.5 hours of stroke symptoms, then thrombolysis can be done, she said, adding: “However, in wake-up stroke, we cannot calculate the time of the onset of symptoms. We do not know the window. So, acting fast is important. In case of any symptoms, patients should reach the hospital on time.”

In wake-up strokes, imaging helps give a clear picture for the doctors. “An MRI brain scan should be taken immediately. If it is not available, a CT angiogram should be taken. The scans help us assess the extent of brain injury and blood flow to different parts of the brain. They can determine whether there is diffusion-perfusion mismatch. The difference may represent brain tissue that is still salvageable and can be potentially saved. Like in regular strokes, ‘time is brain’ in wake-up strokes too, making prompt diagnosis and treatment crucial,” she explained.

Shubha Subramanian, senior consultant - neurology, Kauvery Hospitals, Chennai, said that in ischemic strokes, thrombolysis is used to dissolve the blood clot if a patient presents within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. “In cases involving a large vessel occlusion, mechanical thrombectomy is performed within 24 hours of symptom onset, depending on the patient’s eligibility. In wake-up strokes, we do not know when the stroke started; it could be at night or early in the morning. What we do next is crucial. This is why we rely on imaging techniques,” she added.

“MRI has a lot of sequences. If you compare the diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR (Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery) imaging, a mismatch in that shows that the brain tissue is still salvageable. So even if we do not know the time of onset of stroke, we can still go ahead and thrombolyse the patient. In the same way, MRI perfusion or CT perfusion studies will also give us a clue regarding salvageable brain tissue. This will help us in taking crucial decisions regarding thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy or whether to go for conservative management,” she elaborated.

Under the Tamil Nadu Accident and Emergency Care Initiative and Stroke Care and Rapid Intervention with Plasminogen activator and Thrombectomy (SCRIPT) programme implemented by the Tamil Nadu government and with facilities available at the new JICA building at KMC, patients with with wake-up strokes are regularly treated, Dr. Radha noted.

“There is effective coordination between the administration, the emergency department, radiology and neurology departments. We have a green channel in place. As a result, once the patients with symptoms of stroke enter the Emergency Department, the neurologist is intimated. Our doctor goes to the radiology department which has significantly reduced the door to needle time,” she said.

BE FAST is the acronym to spot the warning signs of stroke, denoting Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech and Time. “We do see that the awareness of stroke symptoms is increasing and the referral system has also improved,” Dr. Radha said.

Dr. Shubha Subramanian said that in wake-up strokes, the person may not realise that he/she has symptoms of stroke when they wake up from sleep. “They may face difficulty in getting up and may also fall as a result. It is important for family members to identify the symptoms and rush for medical help,” she added.

articles.title: Hunker down: On Cyclone Arnab, its landfall
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Proactive governance kept the casualties low after Cyclone Arnab

Cyclone Arnab, the first named storm of the North Indian Ocean cyclone season this year, intensified rapidly before making landfall as a ‘very severe cyclonic storm’ on October 28. This particular rapidity is a challenge for forecasters and some models did fail to anticipate how strong Arnab would become. It also moved faster than expected towards the coast, before stalling for a time and beginning the landfall process several hours before the India Meteorological Department (IMD) had predicted it would, in the middle of the night, leaving many district authorities with a potentially narrower window to evacuate high-risk settlements. With core wind speeds of 125-135 kilometres per hour, it delivered more than 100 mm of rain over parts of Anakapalli, Visakhapatnam, Kalingapatnam, Kakinada and Machilipatnam, in Andhra Pradesh. But even though it has completed landfall, southern Odisha likely faces a greater threat only hence. Early reports claimed no loss of life in Andhra Pradesh or Odisha, which has been attributed to the disaster management operations in both States; the Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister, N. Chandrababu Naidu, said there were five deaths in Andhra Pradesh . Regrettably, the suspension of transport services, including road connectivity and flights, closure of schools and offices, and power cuts to minimise risks posed by loose wires remains an essential part of saving lives, entailing other social and economic disruptions that the States must account for, and address, in their post-storm assessments.

Odisha may have to brace for rainfall and waters due to moisture in the storm’s outer circulation, which will arrive over land that has recovered in patches from the fourth wettest monsoon in the State’s history. Extreme rainfall after repeated flooding may face soil that has not drained fully, raising the risk of more flooding following even lower levels of rainfall, and slope failures in hilly terrain. Farmers in Ganjam and Puri have already voiced worries about the risk of prolonged inundation destroying paddy crops, compounding the already considerable financial consequences of the southwest monsoon; Ganjam alone had lost 33% of crops by October. In Sundargarh, however, farmers hope that Arnab will relieve moisture stress in standing crops after a dry month. The IMD has already issued alerts in the Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Koraput, Malkangiri, Nabarangpur, and Kalahandi districts, before the rainbelt extends further north. The relatively low figure of deaths will be a testament to proactive governance. However, it is past time that States adopted a zero-disruption approach, especially since property and infrastructure were damaged, and the risk of people being pushed into poverty over lost possessions and livelihoods persists.

articles.title: Clinging on: On Netanyahu and the Israel elections
articles.examRelevance: UPSC, State PSC, SSC & Banking Mains: Deep Analytical Core Summary, Policy Critique, 4 Hinglish Vocab & 2 Ultra Premium Analytical Questions
fullParagraphs: Netanyahu’s continuance will be bad news for Israel and the region

Benjamin Netanyahu was at the centre of Israel’s October 27 elections. For Israel’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who oversaw a genocidal war in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7 attack , the election was the biggest test of his political career. For the Opposition, which promised to hold him accountable for the failures of October 7 and end the country’s “forever wars”, the election offered an opportunity to oust him from power. The results, however, sent a mixed message. With 85.6% of the votes counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition has lost its majority but is still the largest bloc . His Likud party is projected to win 26 seats, while its main rival Yashar, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is expected to secure 21. Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, the far-right extremist parties in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, demonstrated their continued strength, winning 13 seats between them. The dark horse, however, could be the Arab parties — the Joint List is projected to win 12 seats while the United Arab List (Ra’am) could secure seven seats. With neither bloc commanding a majority, the Arab parties could propel the opposition coalition to power. But the big question is whether the anti-Netanyahu coalition is ready to join hands with the Arab parties, which have historically been kept on the margins of Israel’ s power politics.

Mr. Netanyahu’s central promise has been that only he can guarantee Israel’s security. Yet, the October 7 attack took place on his watch and he has refused to take responsibility for the failures that led to it. A wanted man by the International Criminal Court, he has repeated, before and after October 7, that a Palestine state would not be formed while he is in power. His war on Gaza has killed over 70,000 Palestinians, including 20,000 children, and displaced the region’s population. Israel’s brutal occupation machinery has also expanded and tightened its control of the West Bank, while settler terrorists have unleashed violence on Palestinian households. His war on Iran has been a disaster, with global economic consequences. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to portray his wars as bold, necessary moves to protect Israel, while exploiting Israelis’ security concerns for political gain. He may not be voted out immediately, but his failure to secure a majority and the decline in his party’s popularity are significant. The Opposition should take its cue from the results and form a broad coalition with the Arab parties. It should restore accountability in governance, revisit his unchecked militarism and rebuild ties with the world. If Mr. Netanyahu continues to cling to power, it would be bad news for Israel and the region.

Netanyahu’s continuance will be bad news for Israel and the region

Benjamin Netanyahu was at the centre of Israel’s October 27 elections. For Israel’s longest-serving Prime Minister, who oversaw a genocidal war in Gaza following Hamas’s October 7 attack , the election was the biggest test of his political career. For the Opposition, which promised to hold him accountable for the failures of October 7 and end the country’s “forever wars”, the election offered an opportunity to oust him from power. The results, however, sent a mixed message. With 85.6% of the votes counted, Mr. Netanyahu’s right-religious coalition has lost its majority but is still the largest bloc . His Likud party is projected to win 26 seats, while its main rival Yashar, led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, is expected to secure 21. Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, the far-right extremist parties in Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition, demonstrated their continued strength, winning 13 seats between them. The dark horse, however, could be the Arab parties — the Joint List is projected to win 12 seats while the United Arab List (Ra’am) could secure seven seats. With neither bloc commanding a majority, the Arab parties could propel the opposition coalition to power. But the big question is whether the anti-Netanyahu coalition is ready to join hands with the Arab parties, which have historically been kept on the margins of Israel’ s power politics.

Mr. Netanyahu’s central promise has been that only he can guarantee Israel’s security. Yet, the October 7 attack took place on his watch and he has refused to take responsibility for the failures that led to it. A wanted man by the International Criminal Court, he has repeated, before and after October 7, that a Palestine state would not be formed while he is in power. His war on Gaza has killed over 70,000 Palestinians, including 20,000 children, and displaced the region’s population. Israel’s brutal occupation machinery has also expanded and tightened its control of the West Bank, while settler terrorists have unleashed violence on Palestinian households. His war on Iran has been a disaster, with global economic consequences. Mr. Netanyahu has sought to portray his wars as bold, necessary moves to protect Israel, while exploiting Israelis’ security concerns for political gain. He may not be voted out immediately, but his failure to secure a majority and the decline in his party’s popularity are significant. The Opposition should take its cue from the results and form a broad coalition with the Arab parties. It should restore accountability in governance, revisit his unchecked militarism and rebuild ties with the world. If Mr. Netanyahu continues to cling to power, it would be bad news for Israel and the region.

articles.title: Karnataka High Court flags irony: Law meant to curb red tapism bogged down it
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Karnataka Conduct of Government Litigation Act, 2023, prescribes that officers must stick to the period of limitation fixed to prefer appeals, review or revision against a court verdict, the Bench said, noting that none of the present appeals demonstrate adherence to the statutory discipline contemplated in the law

Noticing delays from 466 days to 1,099 days in filling appeals against judgments, the High Court of Karnataka has said that the State government enacted the Karnataka Conduct of Government Litigation Act, 2023, “to arrest red tapism, but red tapism appears to have arrested the operation of this law.”

A Division Bench comprising Justice M. Nagaprasanna and Justice Hema Kulkarni made these observations on the four appeals filed by the State government challenging verdicts of a single judge related to service of certain employees in the Karnataka State Law University.

Apart from various judgments of the apex court on delay in filling appeals by the State authorities, the State-enacted Act of 2023 clearly prescribes that officers must stick to the period of limitation fixed to prefer appeals, review or revision against a court verdict, the Bench said, while pointing out that that none of present appeals demonstrate adherence to the statutory discipline contemplated in the law on conduct of litigation.

“The time limits prescribed for movement of files, securing opinions, and taking decisions appear to have been thrown to the winds. The State, which enacted the law to bring order and accountability into governmental litigation, has itself failed to demonstrate fidelity to its mandate. The irony is unmistakable: the State enacted a law to arrest red tapism, but red tapism appears to have arrested the operation of the law, Bench observed.

The Bench noted that the explanations offered for the delays — files moving from table to table, correspondence passing from officer to officer, legal opinions being sought and documents collected — merely chronicled administrative activity without establishing sufficient cause to condone the delay in filling of the appeal.

“The State is expected to be a model litigant, not a privileged procrastinator. Its obligation is to uphold the rule of law, not to seek exceptions from its operation,” the Bench said while observing that “a law enacted by the State cannot remain a mere ornament in the statute book, commanding obedience from everyone except its own author.

Stating that applications filed by the State government explaining reason for the enormous delay “disclose no exceptional circumstance, no compelling impediment and no credible explanation that could constitute sufficient cause for the extraordinary delays,” the Bench said, while observing that “what is presented as an explanation is, in substance, an assortment of administrative excuses; what is sought as judicial indulgence would, if granted, amount to judicial endorsement of bureaucratic apathy.”
Terming one of the applications a “verbatim reproduction” of another, the Bench said a “copy-and-paste explanation cannot become a passport to condonation of delay”.

articles.title: ‘RSS Friends’ registers in U.S. to step up outreach, correct inaccuracies
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: The RSS Friends, which provided a Georgia address in the registration document, listed Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, Keshavkunj, New Delhi as its “foreign principal”
A group of RSS well-wishers has registered with the U.S. Department of Justice as a foreign agent of the organisation, aiming to step up outreach in the U.S.
The RSS Friends, which provided a Georgia address in the registration document, listed Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, Keshavkunj, New Delhi as its “foreign principal”.
The RSS Friends registered with the Department of Justice under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) on August 27.
Correcting or responding to information that RSS Friends believes is inaccurate, incomplete, or lacking relevant context is also listed among proposed activities.

“RSS Friends does not have a written employment, consulting, lobbying, public-relations, or agency agreement with RSS containing specified deliverables, compensation, or detailed operational instructions,” the group said.

It said the absence of a written contract should not be understood as a representation that no relationship, request, understanding, coordination, authorisation, direction, or other relevant factual connection exists.
“RSS Friends will disclose the actual facts relevant to its activities,” it said.
The group said its proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations, and community engagement activities.

“Consistent with its governing documents and applicable law, it may communicate with members of the public, journalists, media organisations, researchers, academic and policy institutions, community leaders, civil-society organisations, and, where appropriate, government agencies or officials,” the group said.
It described the RSS as an India-based volunteer and social cultural organisation.

The RSS Friends, which provided a Georgia address in the registration document, listed Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, Keshavkunj, New Delhi as its “foreign principal”

A group of RSS well-wishers has registered with the U.S. Department of Justice as a foreign agent of the organisation, aiming to step up outreach in the U.S.

The RSS Friends, which provided a Georgia address in the registration document, listed Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, Keshavkunj, New Delhi as its “foreign principal”.

The RSS Friends registered with the Department of Justice under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA) on August 27.

Correcting or responding to information that RSS Friends believes is inaccurate, incomplete, or lacking relevant context is also listed among proposed activities.

“RSS Friends does not have a written employment, consulting, lobbying, public-relations, or agency agreement with RSS containing specified deliverables, compensation, or detailed operational instructions,” the group said.

It said the absence of a written contract should not be understood as a representation that no relationship, request, understanding, coordination, authorisation, direction, or other relevant factual connection exists.

“RSS Friends will disclose the actual facts relevant to its activities,” it said.

The group said its proposed activities are primarily informational, educational, public-relations, and community engagement activities.

“Consistent with its governing documents and applicable law, it may communicate with members of the public, journalists, media organisations, researchers, academic and policy institutions, community leaders, civil-society organisations, and, where appropriate, government agencies or officials,” the group said.

It described the RSS as an India-based volunteer and social cultural organisation.

articles.title: Unmarried rural youth in Maharashtra plan Statewide stir for government help in getting brides
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Polity: Constitutional Amendments, Supreme Court Judgements, Parliamentary Bills & Governance Schemes
fullParagraphs: Core demands of the youth planning to protest include setting up an all-religion marriage registration bureau under the Social Welfare Department, providing direct financial assistance, creating steady rural employment, and guaranteeing remunerative prices for farm produce

It is not the inflation, unemployment, deletion of names from the voters’ list or corruption that is simmering in rural Maharashtra youth who are gearing up for an agitation. Unlike other Gen Z across India, these youth have an unusual demand – get us brides to marry.

“We are planning not only a Statewide but a nationwide network of boys who are not getting brides to marry and plan a massive agitation,” Kisan Nanaware, a 28-year-old youth from Solapur, told The Hindu .

Mr. Nanaware came into the limelight after he held a dharna demanding bride at the District Collector’s office in September. He fears he may suffer the same fate as thousands of men in rural Solapur in western Maharashtra, pointing out that the issue stretches far beyond men in their early 30s, with some in their 40s and 50s having given up hope of finding a partner.

Youth such as Mr. Nanaware argue that the State must issue an official resolution detailing steps to assist those who are unmarried. Their core demands include setting up an all-religion marriage registration bureau under the Social Welfare Department, providing direct financial assistance, creating steady rural employment, and guaranteeing remunerative prices for farm produce. He warns that if authorities fail to act, the movement could take an aggressive turn.
The politicians who have been facing various kinds of agitations are now facing heat of the unmarried youth.

What was supposed to be a standard campaign stop for the Maharashtra Legislative Council elections in Ashti, Beed district (Marathwada region), took a dramatic turn when an agitated young man seized the microphone from local organisers and voiced an issue cutting across rural Maharashtra for which he wanted an immediate answer from the leaders. “Keep aside all other problems and look at our condition,” he demanded, speaking to a crowd of ruling alliance leaders gathered for the Graduates’ and Teachers’ constituency elections held on October 23. “Many of us, including me, have crossed 30 or 32 and still we are not getting brides. Solve this problem first!”

Leaders of the BJP-led ruling coalition were not entirely surprised by the outburst. Behind the scenes, politicians have been monitoring simmering anger among rural men who find themselves systematically rejected by prospective brides and their families due to falling farm incomes, lack of steady employment, and a skewed gender ratio.

Maharashtra recorded a sex ratio of 899 girls per 1,000 boys during the 2022-24 period, marginally improving from 896 girls in 2012-14 but well below the national average of 918 girls, according to the latest Sample Registration System Statistical Report.

From Ministers to leaders across party lines, veteran leader Sharad Pawar to local gram panchayat sarpanches, young boys are now raising one simple question, “What about our marriage?” No one has answer to this.

“If not leaders, who is going to answer? At least they must solve one problem and this is the pressing one,” said 32-year-old Avinash Shende from Yavatmal in Vidarbha region. Along with farming, he is working on a contract with a private cleaning agency and has not completed his graduation. He added that like him other youth in the region are now galvanising support to take up this issue at the State level. He says the movement would start from gram sabhas in villages.

fullParagraphs: At least 17 districts of southern Odisha affected by heavy rainfall due to cyclonic storm Arnab; Andhra Pradesh records five deaths as CM Naidu announces relief measures

A day after various parts of Telangana received rain under the impact of cyclonic storm Arnab, isolated places in 12 districts are likely to receive thunderstorms accompanied with lightning and gusty winds on Thursday (October 29). The very severe cyclonic storm crossed Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts on Wednesday morning, before weakening into a severe cyclonic storm.

The 12 districts where thunderstorms have been forecast are Kumaram Bheem Asifabad, Mancherial, Rajanna Sircilla, Karimnagar, Peddapalli, Jayashankar Bhupalpally, Mulugu, Bhadradri Kothagudem, Khammam, Mahabubabad, Warangal and Hanumakonda districts, as per the India Meteorological Department-Hyderabad Centre’s latest weather bulletin.

With severe cyclonic storm Arnab making landfall along the Andhra coast, rainfall activity is likely to ease considerably across Keralam. With the rains subsiding, daytime temperatures are expected to rise noticeably across the State. The dry spell is likely to persist until another weather system develops over the Bay of Bengal, with the mercury expected to climb during the intervening period.

Cyclone Arnab brought back grim memories of ‘Cyclone Hudhud’, which battered the city 12 years ago. Although ‘Arnab’ was less severe and did not make landfall in the city, the strong winds through the night, extensive damage to the city’s green cover, uprooted electric poles, prolonged power outages and disrupted mobile network connectivity reminded residents of the destruction caused by Hudhud in October 2014.

Residents took to social media to compare their experiences of the two cyclones. People recalled sleepless nights, prolonged power cuts and following the district administration’s instructions to remain indoors unless faced with an emergency.
Cyclone Arnab triggers memories of Hudhud’s 2014 destruction in Vizag, with power outages, uprooted trees, and renewed warnings.

Telangana Deputy Chief Minister and Energy Minister Bhatti Vikramarka spoke to Andhra Pradesh Energy Minister Gottipati Ravi Kumar over the phone on Wednesday to enquire about the impact of Cyclone Arnab.

Mr. Vikramarka assured Andhra Pradesh of the Telangana government’s full support in dealing with the situation. He said Telangana was ready to provide personnel and essential materials for restoring the damaged power supply infrastructure, if required.

Mr. Ravi Kumar briefed Mr. Vikramarka on the relief and restoration operations being carried out under the guidance of Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and thanked the Telangana government for its support.

Andhra Pradesh State Election Commission (SEC) has postponed polling for the Mandal Parishad Territorial Constituency (MPTC) and Zilla Parishad Territorial Constituency (ZPTC) elections from November 3 to November 5 because the counting of votes for the urban local body (ULB) elections is to be done on November 3 under the revised schedule.

fullParagraphs: Elector-to-population ratio released officially by Karnataka CEO shows under-enrolment of about 64.5 lakh electors, of whom roughly 38.41 lakh are in the 18 to 29 age group.

Around 64.5 lakh electors are potentially missing from the final electoral rolls of Karnataka released after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), based on the Elector-to-Population (E-to-P) ratio of 66.11 released by the office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO).

The State’s E-to-P ratio quoted in the CEO’s statements was calculated as the ratio between the total number of electors on the rolls and the estimated population in 2026 in all age groups, including those below 18 years of age and not eligible to vote.

articles.title: Disinvestment as key economic strategy
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: Given the fact that privatisation of several PSEs is a long journey, calibrated disinvestment could serve as an interim measure

S even months into 2026-27, the fiscal year has been shaped by global uncertainty, high energy prices and worries over a deficient monsoon. Against this backdrop, disinvestment and asset monetisation have helped in navigating a challenging fiscal year. While receipts were already on course to meet the budget target, the government’s approval of the sale of its share in the IDBI Bank on October 14 makes it likely that the target will be exceeded. For the industry and investors, the receipts are a signal of the government’s continued commitment to reforms and a larger role for the private sector. This year so far, the disinvestment trajectory has progressed well, even before the IDBI stake sale. According to DIPAM data, the Centre mobilised ₹62,124 crore in April-September 2026 through disinvestment and asset monetisation, of which ₹55,757 crore came from disinvestment. Net tax revenue rose by a modest 3.4% in April-August 2026 and non-tax revenue by 3.2%, while capital expenditure was up by over 18%. It is a policy choice aimed at unlocking greater value from public assets, widening public ownership, and improving efficiency and governance through greater market discipline. The 2022 LIC IPO which drew in many first-time retail investors and policyholders remains a prime example.

This was precisely the rationale behind the government’s 2021 New Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) Policy which envisages a “bare minimum presence” of PSEs in strategic sectors. A target of ₹16.72 lakh crore has been set under NMP 2.0 for FY26-30 after having achieved 90% of its Phase 1 goal.

It is one of the largest Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) deals in India’s financial sector and constitutes as the first step towards a ‘Privatisation 2.0’ framework. More importantly, this framework is premised on being investor-led, professionally managed and time-bound. Two changes would help to turn into a template.

It would work better to first gauge interest across a wider pool and prioritise PSEs that draw strong bids at expected valuations, with structured investor feedback flagging procedural and regulatory hurdles early. articles.title: U.S. Fed holds interest rates steady despite surging inflation
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & IBPS/SBI/RBI/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP Growth, Inflation, Fiscal Deficit & Trade Balance
fullParagraphs: The 12-member FOMC voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 and 4.00%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation

The US Federal Reserve on Wednesday (October 28, 2026) held interest rates steady, in line with market expectations, days ahead of crucial midterm elections where surging inflation has been a key issue.

The 12-member Federal Open Market Committee voted 10-2 to hold rates at a target range between 3.75 and 4.00%, citing the need for more data in the fight against inflation, after having hiked for the first time in three years at its previous meeting in September.

“The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s two percent goal,” the Fed said in a statement announcing its decision.
Two members of the committee, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, dissented, calling instead for an immediate 0.25-percentage-point rate hike.
The central bank has missed its long-term two-percent target for inflation for more than five years, with households and businesses battered by sustained price increases.

U.S. President Donald Trump's war on Iran, launched in late February, has sent energy prices skyrocketing and fueled domestic inflation, alongside his wide-ranging tariff policies. Prices have also been driven by an investment boom in artificial intelligence (AI) technology and the build-out of huge data centres to support it. The decision comes six days ahead of the November 3 midterm elections, in which the Democratic Party is seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress from Mr. Trump's Republicans. Mr. Trump's handling of the economy has been a key issue throughout the campaign, with working-class households across the country struggling to make ends meet despite largely stable overall economic growth.
U.S. consumer inflation came in hotter than expected in September, clocking in at 3.7%, edging back towards a three-year high established in May.
Still, key policymakers at the Fed -- including Mr. Warsh -- have signalled that they did not see an urgency to raise rates again immediately.

Speaking in Bangkok earlier this month, Mr. Warsh said that U.S. economic conditions had “broadly conformed” to policymakers’ expectations, fueling speculation that the Fed may pause at the October meeting.
On Wednesday (October 28, 2026), the Fed said economic activity in the United States was expanding at a “strong” pace, upgrading its language from the FOMC meeting six weeks prior.

articles.title: Bengaluru-based Nature Classrooms releases new butterfly migration game
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Aswathi Asokan, who has conceptualised this new game, talks about its genesis, how it is played and how gamification can help drive conservation

Aswathi Asokan’s journey into the fascinating world of butterflies began in 2019, as a first-year Zoology student at Chennai’s Stella Maris College. “There were a couple of professors in the Zoology Department who were interested in the natural world,” she says, recalling how one of them, Kalpana Jayaraman, was conducting butterfly walks on campus.
“So I began joining those,” says the Bengaluru-based nature educator, researcher, and conservationist who has conceptualised Monsoon Wings, a new butterfly migration and life-cycle game.

As someone who grew up on the verdant IIT Madras campus, she always loved nature, but “it had never got to the point where I was actively identifying species,” she says. Then, on that first campus walk, the professor gave participants a simple printout of the names and pictures of eight or nine common butterflies.

“That made all the difference. Every time I saw a butterfly, I would go back to the printout and try to identify it,” says Aswathi, who developed Monsoon Wings as part of her role as the manager of curriculum development, resources & training at Nature Classrooms, a Bengaluru-based organisation that works with schools and educators to connect learning and the natural world. “I like to think that this was the start of me understanding the power of a tool like that.”

She began noticing butterflies a lot more after that, closely observing their life cycles in the plants around her. At around the same time, she became part of the Chennai Young Naturalists’ Network, a group of young naturalists in Chennai.

Through this group, she met like-minded people, with whom she would go on to co-author a bilingual field guide, Butterflies of Chennai , in 2023. ”The data used to create the guide came from my friend Vikas Madhav, an experienced young naturalist who did nearly 10 years of butterfly documentation work in Chennai before moving to the US,” says Aswathi, who ended up doing a lot of nature education work in Chennai before going on to pursue a master’s in wildlife conservation action from the Bharati Vidyapeeth Institute of Environment Education and Research, Pune.
Blue Tiger butterflies are known for their seasonal migrations, linked to monsoon cycles | Photo Credit: MURALI KUMAR K

All the time spent dabbling in resource creation, including field guides, bingos and posters, has played a tremendous role in shaping this new butterfly game, which has been inspired by the ‘Bird Survivor’ game by Early Bird, an initiative by the Education and Public Engagement Programme of the Nature Conservation Foundation. “We were using this game extensively in our Nature Classrooms workshops, and I got familiar with it,” Aswathi says, explaining that this game, in turn, took inspiration from one developed by the Cornell Lab of Ornithology.

While working with Nature Classrooms, Aswathi was also actively working with Sunnyside Learning School in Chennai, running biodiversity exploration programmes for its students. “I was trying to plan a session around butterflies for the Sunnyside kids, and since the mechanics are quite similar, I thought I could adapt the bird migration game to a butterfly context and see if it works.”

While bird and monarch butterfly migration are well known and widely discussed, butterfly migration in India is so common right around us, yet few people know about it, Aswathi says. “That’s why I wanted to create a resource and incorporate that into the kids’ session.”

articles.title: India must build a holistic care system
articles.examRelevance: Prelims & GS-III: ISRO/DRDO Missions, Quantum & AI Tech, Biodiversity, Ramsar Sites & Climate Action
fullParagraphs: Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework

India’s development story over the past decade has been one of infrastructure: highways, metro lines, electrification and digital public platforms, each treated as a foundation for growth that requires public investment and planning. One foundation on which every household and economy depends has not received the same attention: care.

Everyone needs care at some point in life. How care is organised shapes people’s opportunities, well-being and participation in society and the economy. When services are absent, families, and women most of all, bear the cost in unpaid work, lost earnings, and narrower opportunities.

In the Periodic Labour Force Survey 2025, 44.4% of women outside the labour force cited childcare and homemaking as the main reason for staying out of the labour force. India’s Time Use Survey 2024 found that 41% of women aged 15–59 provided unpaid care, spending an average of 140 minutes a day on it. Expanding access to affordable, quality care services can give women greater freedom to pursue employment, leisure and participation in public life. With an ageing population, the need for accessible care services will only grow.

Yet care rarely features in India’s growth strategy. For a Viksit Bharat 2047, the question is not only how to expand women’s economic participation, but how to build the care system that makes such participation possible. The Anganwadi network, strengthened through Saksham Anganwadi and POSHAN 2.0, anchors early childhood care and nutrition. Palna, under Mission Shakti, supports crèches, while Mission Vatsalya, social security and provisions for persons with disabilities and senior citizens address other needs. The challenge is architecture, not ambition. Four gaps stand out.

First, fragmentation. Care is split across multiple Ministries, from women and child development to housing and urban affairs. Each runs valuable programmes, but without a common framework. This can leave gaps such as crèches that close before factory shifts end or eldercare needs that fall outside of existing schemes.

Second, coverage. The United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) estimates that 9–10 million women in low-income urban households need childcare. Similarly for eldercare, 24% of older persons face limitations in daily activities, while national data on service availability and coverage remain limited.

Third, the workforce. Care depends on frontline workers; from Anganwadi workers to home-based caregivers and domestic workers — many of whom remain inadequately remunerated or engaged on an honorary basis. Building on NITI Aayog’s proposals, clear standards, certification, decent working conditions, social protection and career pathways would recognise care as skilled and paid work.

Finally, financing and norms. Care is still budgeted as welfare rather than investment, and workplace policies assume that caregiving is women’s work. The Economic Advisory Council to the Prime Minister (EAC-PM) recommends statutory paid paternity leave in the private sector.

Comparable economies are building their own care ecosystems. Colombia’s 2025 National Care Policy brings 34 government entities under one framework. Brazil’s 2024 National Care Policy and 2025 National Care Plan set up inter-Ministerial committees to steer implementation. In Nepal, care mapping was used to fund care pilots.

In India, NITI Aayog’s Reimagining Care: Strategies for Empowering Caregivers in Viksit Bharat@2047 report proposes a National Caregiving Council to strengthen coordination. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is consulting States and Union Territories; its May 2026 national workshop discussed a National Care Economy Mission with inter-Ministerial governance, aligned financing and shared data. State-level care roadmaps can make this practical. States can map needs, services and demographic trends, identify gaps in childcare, eldercare and disability support, and prepare costed plans with clear responsibilities.
